claim: SNPs near lymphatic endothelial marker gene loci (VEGFC, LYVE1, FLT4) are associated with cardiovascular and metabolic phenotypes including cardiac hypertrophy in humans.
source: Interestingly, several SNPs near lymphatic endothelial markers VEGFC, LYVE1, FLT4 loci are associated with cardiovascular and metabolic phenotypes including cardiac hypertrophy in humans (Fung et al., 2019; Johansson et al., 2010; justice et al., 2019; Kettunen et al., 2016; Kichaev et al., 2019; Lotta et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2017; Nasa Sinnott-Armstrong et al., 2019; Saxena et al., 2010; van der Harst and Verweij, 2018; Wild et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2018; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple GWAS studies and reference to Table 1 which lists specific SNPs and their associations.

claim: VEGFC expression is reduced by 19.6% on average in hearts from chronic heart failure patients compared with hearts from healthy donors.
source: A significant (19.6% for VEGFC, 38.8% for LYVE1 and 21.7% for FLT4 on average) reduction was observed for lymphatic markers VEGFC, LYVE1, and FLT4, and a 31.6% reduction was observed in PDPN (p=0.07) in hearts from chronic heart failure patients compared with hearts from healthy donors (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from human heart samples shown in Figure 1 and quantified in the text.

claim: LYVE1 expression is reduced by 38.8% on average in hearts from chronic heart failure patients compared with hearts from healthy donors.
source: A significant (19.6% for VEGFC, 38.8% for LYVE1 and 21.7% for FLT4 on average) reduction was observed for lymphatic markers VEGFC, LYVE1, and FLT4, and a 31.6% reduction was observed in PDPN (p=0.07) in hearts from chronic heart failure patients compared with hearts from healthy donors (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from human heart samples shown in Figure 1 and quantified in the text.

claim: FLT4 expression is reduced by 21.7% on average in hearts from chronic heart failure patients compared with hearts from healthy donors.
source: A significant (19.6% for VEGFC, 38.8% for LYVE1 and 21.7% for FLT4 on average) reduction was observed for lymphatic markers VEGFC, LYVE1, and FLT4, and a 31.6% reduction was observed in PDPN (p=0.07) in hearts from chronic heart failure patients compared with hearts from healthy donors (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from human heart samples shown in Figure 1 and quantified in the text.

claim: PDPN expression is reduced by 31.6% (p=0.07) in hearts from chronic heart failure patients compared with hearts from healthy donors.
source: A significant (19.6% for VEGFC, 38.8% for LYVE1 and 21.7% for FLT4 on average) reduction was observed for lymphatic markers VEGFC, LYVE1, and FLT4, and a 31.6% reduction was observed in PDPN (p=0.07) in hearts from chronic heart failure patients compared with hearts from healthy donors (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from human heart samples shown in Figure 1 and quantified in the text.

claim: VEGFCc156s specifically activates VEGFR3 but not VEGFR2 in vitro.
source: To induce lymphangiogenesis in this model, we used the lymphangiogenic growth factor mutant VEGFCc156s, which specifically activates vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 3 (VEGFR3) but not vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) in vitro (Joukov et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joukov et al., 1998.

claim: VEGFCc156s enhances lymphangiogenesis in vivo.
source: To induce lymphangiogenesis in this model, we used the lymphangiogenic growth factor mutant VEGFCc156s, which specifically activates vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 3 (VEGFR3) but not vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) in vitro (Joukov et al., 1998) and enhances lymphangiogenesis in vivo (Klotz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klotz et al., 2015.

claim: VEGFCc156s has a short half-life in plasma.
source: Pharmacokinetic analysis of single subcutaneous dosing of VEGFCc156s indicated that VEGFCc156s has a short half-life in plasma (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacokinetic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VEGFCc156s infusion maintained a 1.9-fold average increase in plasma VEGFC concentration in treated mice compared with control mice.
source: The VEGFCc156s infusion was calculated to maintain a two-fold increase in plasma VEGFC concentration, and the analysis at endpoint confirmed a significant 1.9-fold average increase in plasma VEGFC concentration in the treated mice compared with control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring plasma VEGFC concentration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion induced cardiac hypertrophy and impaired cardiac contractility.
source: Echocardiography was conducted at endpoint to examine cardiac function, and the results indicated that angiotensin II infusion induced cardiac hypertrophy and impaired cardiac contractility.
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiography data referenced in the text and shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment prevented angiotensin II-induced impairments in cardiac function.
source: In contrast, VEGFCc156s treatment prevented angiotensin II-induced impairments in cardiac function (Figure 2B–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 2B-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-1G.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion significantly increased heart weight and lung weight.
source: Consistent with the echocardiography results, angiotensin II infusion also significantly increased heart weight and lung weight, which possibly reflects an increase in lung edema (King and Goldstein, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on heart and lung weights, with a citation suggesting the interpretation of lung weight increase.

claim: VEGFCc156s prevented the angiotensin II-induced increases in heart and lung weights.
source: whereas VEGFCc156s prevented the angiotensin II-induced increases in heart and lung weights (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Angiotensin II treatment significantly increased Nppb expression in mouse hearts compared with control hearts.
source: Moreover, gene expression analysis revealed a significant increase in the expression of Nppb, encoding heart failure marker B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), in angiotensin II-treated mouse hearts compared with control hearts
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: VEGFCc156s significantly decreased Nppb expression in angiotensin II-infused hearts.
source: while VEGFCc156s significantly decreased Nppb expression in angiotensin II-infused hearts (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion significantly increased cardiomyocyte size and heterogeneity.
source: Whereas angiotensin II infusion significantly increased cardiomyocyte size and heterogeneity
evidence: The claim is supported by wheat germ agglutinin staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-1J.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment prevented the change in cell size heterogeneity in angiotensin II-infused mouse hearts.
source: VEGFCc156s treatment prevented the change in cell size heterogeneity in angiotensin II-infused mouse hearts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–1J)
evidence: The claim is supported by wheat germ agglutinin staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-1J.

claim: A significant reduction in lymphatic endothelial marker podoplanin expression was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts compared with control hearts.
source: Similar to what was observed in human hearts (Figure 1), a significant reduction in lymphatic endothelial marker podoplanin expression was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts compared with control hearts
evidence: The claim is supported by protein expression analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment restored podoplanin expression in angiotensin II-infused hearts back to control level.
source: Interestingly, VEGFCc156s treatment restored podoplanin expression in angiotensin II-infused hearts back to control level, indicating that VEGFCc156s treatment may prevent the loss of cardiac lymphatic vessels during cardiac dysfunction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein expression analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: Immunohistochemistry revealed a significant reduction in podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel density in angiotensin II-infused hearts.
source: Consistent with the protein expression analysis, immunohistochemistry revealed a significant reduction in podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel density in angiotensin II-infused hearts, which was restored by VEGFCc156s treatment (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment restored podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel density in angiotensin II-infused hearts.
source: Consistent with the protein expression analysis, immunohistochemistry revealed a significant reduction in podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel density in angiotensin II-infused hearts, which was restored by VEGFCc156s treatment (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel lumen area was significantly increased in the hearts of VEGFCc156s + angiotensin II-infused animals compared with animals treated with angiotensin II alone.
source: More interestingly, podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel lumen area was significantly increased in the hearts of VEGFCc156s + angiotensin II-infused animals compared with animals that had been treated with angiotensin II alone, indicating that VEGFCc156s may improve lymphatic transport function in diseased animals (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment increased phospho-Akt levels in hearts compared with control or angiotensin II-infused hearts.
source: Consistent with the ability of VEGFC to activate Akt and Erk pathways, we observed increased phospho-Akt levels and a trend towards an increase in phospho-Erk in VEGFCc156s-treated hearts compared with control or angiotensin II-infused hearts
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K, M and N.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly increased lymphatic vessel diameter in the ear skin of treated animals.
source: Similar to its effects on cardiac lymphatic vessels, VEGFCc156s treatment also significantly increased lymphatic vessel diameter and lymphatic vascular density in the ear skin of treated animals, supporting a systemic lymphangiogenic response induced by VEGFCc156s treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1O–1R).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1O-1R.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly increased lymphatic vascular density in the ear skin of treated animals.
source: Similar to its effects on cardiac lymphatic vessels, VEGFCc156s treatment also significantly increased lymphatic vessel diameter and lymphatic vascular density in the ear skin of treated animals, supporting a systemic lymphangiogenic response induced by VEGFCc156s treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1O–1R).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1O-1R.

claim: Angiotensin II treatment induced vascular leakage, leading to interstitial accumulation of cadaverine in angiotensin II-infused hearts.
source: Angiotensin II treatment induced vascular leakage, leading to interstitial accumulation of cadaverine in angiotensin II-infused hearts.
evidence: The claim is supported by lymphangiography data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: VEGFCc156s-treated, angiotensin II-infused animals showed significantly reduced cadaverine accumulation in heart.
source: In contrast, VEGFCc156s-treated, angiotensin II-infused animals showed significantly reduced cadaverine accumulation in heart, indicating reduced leakage and improved fluid clearance (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by lymphangiography data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Plasma qdot concentration demonstrated a significant decrease in angiotensin II-infused mice compared with control mice, indicating impaired cardiac lymphatic transport.
source: However, quantification of the plasma qdot concentration, which is an indirect parameter to evaluate cardiac lymphatic transport efficiency, demonstrated a significant decrease in angiotensin II-infused mice compared with control mice, indicating impaired cardiac lymphatic transport.
evidence: The claim is supported by lymphangiography data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment in the angiotensin II-infused mice significantly increased the plasma qdot concentration compared with the angiotensin II-infused mice, indicating improved cardiac lymphatic transport.
source: Conversely, VEGFCc156s treatment in the angiotensin II-infused mice significantly increased the plasma qdot concentration compared with the angiotensin II-infused mice, indicating improved cardiac lymphatic transport (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by lymphangiography data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A trend toward an increased heart wet-to-dry weight ratio was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts.
source: Concomitantly, a trend toward an increased heart wet-to-dry weight ratio was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts, which was significantly reduced with VEGFCc156s treatment
evidence: The claim is supported by gravimetry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced the heart wet-to-dry weight ratio in angiotensin II-infused hearts.
source: Concomitantly, a trend toward an increased heart wet-to-dry weight ratio was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts, which was significantly reduced with VEGFCc156s treatment, indicating improved regulation of cardiac fluid balance in VEGFCc156s-treated mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gravimetry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion upregulated the expression of multiple genes involved in inflammation, chemotaxis and related pathways in LECs from both heart and diaphragm.
source: Notably, angiotensin II infusion upregulated the expression of multiple genes involved in inflammation, chemotaxis and related pathways in LECs from both heart and diaphragm.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment downregulated the expression of inflammatory and chemotactic genes in LECs.
source: Conversely, VEGFCc156s treatment downregulated the expression of these inflammatory and chemotactic genes (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: A significant 43% increase in plasma KC/GRO levels was noted in angiotensin II-infused mice compared with control mice.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq analysis, a significant 43% increase in plasma KC/GRO levels was noted in angiotensin II-infused mice compared with control mice
evidence: The claim is supported by chemokine measurement data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment trended to reduce plasma KC/GRO levels in angiotensin II-infused mice.
source: and VEGFCc156s treatment trended to reduce plasma KC/GRO levels in angiotensin II-infused mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemokine measurement data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Significantly increased levels of IP-10 (37.2% increase), MDC (68% increase), and KC/GRO (30% increase) were observed in skin of angiotensin II-infused mice compared with control mice.
source: Furthermore, we observed significantly increased levels of several chemokines (37.2% for chemokine interferon γ-induced protein 10 (IP-10), 68% for macrophage-derived chemokine (MDC) and 30% for KC/GRO on average) in skin of angiotensin II-infused mice compared with control mice
evidence: The claim is supported by chemokine measurement data shown in Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced the levels or induced a trend toward a reduction in chemokines (IP-10, MDC, KC/GRO) in skin.
source: while VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced the levels or induced a trend toward a reduction in these chemokines (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemokine measurement data shown in Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion significantly increased general macrophage density in heart as well as macrophage density near arteries.
source: In addition, angiotensin II infusion significantly increased general macrophage density in heart as well as macrophage density near arteries as assessed by CD68 immunostaining, indicating increased local macrophage content
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced macrophage density in heart.
source: whereas VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced these parameters (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: VEGFCc156s-treated, angiotensin II-infused mice showed a similar significant increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure as those that were treated with angiotensin II alone in the first week.
source: Interestingly, VEGFCc156s-treated, angiotensin II-infused mice showed a similar significant increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure as those that were treated with angiotensin II alone in the first week.
evidence: The claim is supported by telemetry data shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: Starting at week 2, the VEGFCc156s-treated angiotensin II group demonstrated a gradual return in systolic and diastolic blood pressure that was comparable to control mice by week 4.
source: However, starting at week 2, the VEGFCc156s-treated angiotensin II group demonstrated a gradual return in systolic and diastolic blood pressure that was comparable to control mice by week 4 (Figure 5B–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by telemetry data shown in Figure 5B-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both angiotensin II-infused mice and VEGFCc156s-treated, angiotensin II-infused mice showed a significant increase in pulse wave velocity compared with control mice.
source: To examine whether VEGFCc156s alleviated angiotensin II infusion-mediated aortic remodeling to reduce blood pressure, pulse wave velocity was assessed to examine aortic stiffness, and both angiotensin II-infused mice and VEGFCc156s-treated, angiotensin II-infused mice showed a significant increase in pulse wave velocity compared with control mice
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse wave velocity data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment did not alter angiotensin II infusion-mediated aortic stiffness and remodeling.
source: indicating that VEGFCc156s treatment did not alter angiotensin II infusion-mediated aortic stiffness and remodeling (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse wave velocity data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The expression of renal Ace2 mRNA was induced in both angiotensin II-infused mice and VEGFCc156s-treated, angiotensin II-infused mice to a similar extent compared with the kidneys from control mice.
source: In addition, the expression of renal Ace2 mRNA, which encodes the degradation enzyme for angiotensin II, was induced in both angiotensin II-infused mice and VEGFCc156s-treated, angiotensin II-infused mice to a similar extent compared with the kidneys from control mice, indicating a similar compensatory response in kidney to cope with continuous angiotensin II infusion (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion induced vascular hypertrophy in the kidney of both angiotensin II-infused and VEGFCc156s-treated angiotensin II-infused animals.
source: Based on the evaluation of hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) stained sections by a veterinary pathologist, angiotensin II infusion induced vascular hypertrophy in the kidney of both angiotensin II-infused and VEGFCc156s-treated angiotensin II-infused animals, which is consistent with the putative action of angiotensin II as a vasoactive molecule (Mehta and Griendling, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological evaluation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B, with a citation supporting the interpretation.

claim: Angiotensin II-infused VEGFCc156s-treated animals showed a reduced incidence of angiotensin II-induced secondary disturbances such as interstitial mononuclear cell infiltrates and tubular basophilia in the kidney compared with angiotensin II-infused animals.
source: However, angiotensin II-infused VEGFCc156s-treated animals showed a reduced incidence of angiotensin II-induced secondary disturbances such as interstitial mononuclear cell infiltrates and tubular basophilia in the kidney compared with angiotensin II-infused animals, indicating that VEGFCc156s treatment partially alleviated angiotensin II infusion-induced kidney injury (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological evaluation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced the total and perivascular PSR-positive area in kidneys of angiotensin II-infused mice.
source: In addition, picrosirius red (PSR) staining demonstrated increased fibrosis with angiotensin II infusion, and VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced the total and perivascular PSR-positive area in kidneys of angiotensin II-infused mice, indicating that VEGFCc156s treatment alleviated angiotensin II-induced kidney fibrosis and injury (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, C and D.

claim: A significant increase in urine volume was observed in angiotensin II-infused mice compared with control mice over 24 hr.
source: Moreover, a significant increase in urine volume was observed in angiotensin II-infused mice compared with control mice over 24 hr
evidence: The claim is supported by urine collection data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The angiotensin II-infused, VEGFCc156s-treated mice displayed a significant reduction in urine volume.
source: while the angiotensin II-infused, VEGFCc156s-treated mice displayed a significant reduction in urine volume (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by urine collection data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion caused kidney damage and significantly increased the amount of non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA), total urinary protein, and the albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR).
source: Urine composition was also evaluated, and consistent with the pathological evaluation, angiotensin II infusion caused kidney damage and significantly increased the amount of non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA), total urinary protein, and the albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by urine biochemistry data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced NEFA, total urinary protein, and ACR compared with animals that had been treated with angiotensin II alone.
source: In contrast, VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced these parameters compared with animals that had been treated with angiotensin II alone, suggesting that VEGFCc156s treatment alleviated angiotensin II-induced kidney damage.
evidence: The claim is supported by urine biochemistry data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion significantly increased the mRNA expression levels of lymphatic endothelial markers Lyve1, Pdpn, Vegfc, and Flt4 in kidney.
source: Angiotensin II infusion significantly increased the mRNA expression levels of lymphatic endothelial markers Lyve1, Pdpn, Vegfc, and Flt4 in kidney, which is consistent with previous reports (Balasubbramanian et al., 2020; Lopez Gelston et al., 2018) and represents an endogenous expansion in response to systemic hypertension.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F, with citations to previous reports.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced lymphatic endothelial marker expression in angiotensin II-infused mouse kidneys to levels that were comparable to control mice.
source: Surprisingly, VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced, rather than increased, lymphatic endothelial marker expression in angiotensin II-infused mouse kidneys to levels that were comparable to control mice (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Immunohistochemistry showed a trend toward increased Lyve1-positive lymphatic vessel density in angiotensin II-infused kidneys.
source: Consistent with the gene expression analysis, immunohistochemistry also showed a trend toward increased Lyve1-positive lymphatic vessel density in angiotensin II-infused kidneys
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment ameliorated the increase in Lyve1-positive lymphatic vessel density in angiotensin II-infused kidneys.
source: and VEGFCc156s treatment ameliorated this response (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: VEGFCc156s infusion increased plasma VEGFC concentration in animals treated with VEGFCc156s alone as well as in animals treated with angiotensin II and VEGFCc156s at 1 week after treatment.
source: As expected, VEGFCc156s infusion increased plasma VEGFC concentration in animals treated with VEGFCc156s alone as well as in animals treated with angiotensin II and VEGFCc156s similarly as was observed in the longer study (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Significant and comparable increases in hemoglobin levels and hematocrit percentage were observed in the angiotensin II-infused animals compared with the control groups at 1 week.
source: Significant and comparable increases in hemoglobin levels and hematocrit percentage were observed in the angiotensin II-infused animals compared with the control groups, consistent with an increase in blood pressure in angiotensin II-infused groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by hemoglobin and hematocrit measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Renal Ace2 mRNA expression was similarly induced in both angiotensin II-infused groups compared with the control groups at 1 week.
source: As an additional control, we examined renal Ace2 mRNA expression and confirmed its similar induction in both angiotensin II-infused groups compared with the control groups, indicating induction of a compensatory response in the kidney and further validating the action of angiotensin II on both treatment groups at endpoint (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No significant change in urinary ACR was observed among the groups at 1 week after angiotensin II infusion.
source: Kidney function was examined in these animals by measuring urinary ACR, and no significant change was observed among the groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), indicating that the animals had not developed significant kidney dysfunction with a 7-day angiotensin II infusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by urine biochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: No significant change in kidney lymphatic endothelial marker Lyve1 expression and lyve1-positive lymphatic vessel density was found among the groups at 1 week.
source: We further evaluated kidney expression of lymphatic endothelial marker Lyve1 as well as lyve1-positive lymphatic vessel density and found no significant change in both parameters among the groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–1H), indicating renal lymphangiogenesis was not yet observed with a 7-day infusion of angiotensin II or VEGFCc156s.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F-1H.

claim: No significant changes in lyve1-positive lymphatic vessel density in skin were observed at 1 week.
source: We found no significant changes in lyve1-positive lymphatic vessel density in skin at this time point (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: Animals treated with VEGFCc156s alone or in combination with angiotensin II showed a significant increase in podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel density in heart at 1 week.
source: However, animals treated with VEGFCc156s alone or in combination with angiotensin II showed a significant increase in podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessel density in heart compared with other groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1K and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: A significant increase in left ventricular mass and ventricular wall thickness in angiotensin II-infused mice was observed at 1 week after angiotensin II infusion.
source: While echocardiography demonstrated no significant change in cardiac contractility among the animals, a significant increase in left ventricular mass and ventricular wall thickness in angiotensin II-infused mice was observed, indicating the development of cardiac hypertrophy at 1 week after angiotensin II infusion (Figure 7B–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1M–1O).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 7B-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1M-1O.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment did not significantly alleviate angiotensin II-induced cardiac hypertrophy at 1 week after treatment by echocardiography.
source: Interestingly, VEGFCc156s treatment did not significantly alleviate angiotensin II-induced cardiac hypertrophy at 1 week after treatment by echocardiography.
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: A significant increase in heart weight and a trend towards increased lung weight were observed in angiotensin II-infused animals compared with the control groups at 1 week.
source: Similarly, a significant increase in heart weight and a trend towards increased lung weight were observed in angiotensin II-infused animals compared with the control groups
evidence: The claim is supported by organ weight data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment did not alter heart and lung weights in angiotensin II-infused animals at 1 week.
source: and VEGFCc156s treatment did not alter heart and lung weights in angiotensin II-infused animals at this time point (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by organ weight data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: A significant increase in nppb mRNA expression was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts at 1 week.
source: Despite the lack of alterations in cardiac function with 7 days of VEGFCc156s infusion, a significant increase in nppb mRNA expression was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment restored nppb expression in angiotensin II-infused hearts back to a level that was comparable with the control hearts at 1 week.
source: and VEGFCc156s treatment restored nppb expression in angiotensin II-infused hearts back to a level that was comparable with the control hearts (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: A significant increase in the mRNA expression of profibrotic markers (Col1a1, Col1a2, Col3a1 and Fn1) was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts compared with control hearts at 1 week.
source: Furthermore, a significant increase in the mRNA expression of profibrotic markers (Col1a1, Col1a2, Col3a1 and Fn1) was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts compared with control hearts
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7I and J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1P and Q.

claim: Animals that had also been treated with VEGFCc156s demonstrated a significant reduction in the expression of profibrotic markers at 1 week.
source: while animals that had also been treated with VEGFCc156s demonstrated a significant reduction in the expression of these markers (Figure 7I and J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1P and Q)
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7I and J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1P and Q.

claim: Angiotensin II-infused hearts showed a significant increase in PSR-positive area at 1 week, indicating the development of cardiac fibrosis.
source: Consistent with the gene expression analyses, angiotensin II-infused hearts showed a significant increase in PSR-positive area, indicating the development of cardiac fibrosis
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7K and L.

claim: VEGFCc156s induced a trend toward a reduced PSR-positive area percentage in angiotensin II-infused hearts at 1 week.
source: while VEGFCc156s induced a trend toward a reduced PSR-positive area percentage in angiotensin II-infused hearts (Figure 7K and L)
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7K and L.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion for 7 days significantly increased the mRNA expression of multiple inflammatory markers, cytokines, and chemokines.
source: Gene expression analyses of proinflammatory markers revealed that angiotensin II infusion for 7 days significantly increased the mRNA expression of multiple inflammatory markers, cytokines, and chemokines (Figure 7M, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7M and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-2I.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly decreased the expression of proinflammatory markers in angiotensin II-infused hearts at 1 week.
source: Conversely, VEGFC156s treatment significantly decreased the expression of these proinflammatory markers in angiotensin II-infused hearts, suggesting that VEGFCc156s alleviated angiotensin II-induced cardiac inflammation.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7M and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-2I.

claim: A significant increase in CD68-positive macrophage density was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts compared with control hearts at 1 week.
source: A significant increase in CD68-positive macrophage density was observed in angiotensin II-infused hearts compared with control hearts
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7N and Figure 7—figure supplement 2J.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced CD68-positive macrophage density in angiotensin II-infused hearts at 1 week.
source: and VEGFCc156s treatment significantly reduced CD68-positive macrophage density in angiotensin II-infused hearts (Figure 7N, Figure 7—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7N and Figure 7—figure supplement 2J.

claim: The lymphatic vasculature plays an important role in mediating fluid balance and local inflammation in many tissues and organs throughout the body.
source: The lymphatic vasculature plays an important role in mediating fluid balance and local inflammation in many tissues and organs throughout the body (Huang et al., 2017; Oliver et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The heart carries a complex lymphatic network and relies on cardiac lymphatics to drain interstitial fluids and immune cells for maintaining homeostasis.
source: The heart also carries a complex lymphatic network and relies on cardiac lymphatics to drain interstitial fluids and immune cells for maintaining homeostasis (Brakenhielm and Alitalo, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Disrupting cardiac lymphatics can cause myocardial edema and lead to impaired cardiac function.
source: Disrupting cardiac lymphatics can cause myocardial edema and lead to impaired cardiac function (Cui et al., 2001; Mehlhorn et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Therapeutic lymphangiogenesis reduced myocardial edema and fibrosis, resolved inflammation, and improved cardiac function after myocardial infarction in rodent models.
source: Several studies have demonstrated using rodent models that therapeutic lymphangiogenesis reduced myocardial edema and fibrosis, resolved inflammation, and improved cardiac function after myocardial infarction (Henri et al., 2016; Houssari et al., 2020; Klotz et al., 2015; Tatin et al., 2017; Trincot et al., 2019; Vieira et al., 2018) or ischemia and reperfusion injury (Shimizu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Angiotensin II promotes cardiac dysfunction directly via its effects on cardiomyocytes.
source: To examine the role of the lymphatic vasculature in cardiac dysfunction further, we used a model of angiotensin II infusion, which promotes cardiac dysfunction directly via its effects on cardiomyocytes (Mazzolai et al., 2000; Mehta and Griendling, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Angiotensin II promotes cardiac dysfunction indirectly by its action on the renin-angiotensin system to induce hypertension.
source: and indirectly by its action on the renin-angiotensin system to induce hypertension (Mehta and Griendling, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VEGFCc156s can directly enhance lymphatic pump activity and lymphatic output in rat mesentery collecting lymphatics.
source: Moreover, VEGFCc156s can reportedly directly enhance lymphatic pump activity and lymphatic output in rat mesentery collecting lymphatics (Breslin et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Myocardial edema is a key clinical feature of cardiac dysfunction and chronic heart failure.
source: Myocardial edema is a key clinical feature of cardiac dysfunction and chronic heart failure, and heart function could be significantly compromised with a subtle increase in interstitial fluid volume (Dongaonkar et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Angiotensin II can induce endothelial dysfunction.
source: Likely the impairments in lymphatic vascular function observed in angiotensin II-infused mice could come directly from angiotensin II actions on the endothelium, as angiotensin II can induce endothelial dysfunction (Gomolak and Didion, 2014; Watanabe et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hypertension reportedly alters lymphatic vascular function.
source: or perhaps indirectly from angiotensin II infusion-induced hypertension, which reportedly alters lymphatic vascular function (Dongaonkar et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Angiotensin II initiates inflammatory and chemotactic responses in tissues and vasculature.
source: Our RNA-seq analysis indicated that LECs expressed proinflammatory chemokines after angiotensin II stimulation (Figure 4), which is consistent with previous reports indicating a role of angiotensin II in initiating inflammatory and chemotactic responses in tissues and vasculature (Benigni et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VEGFCc156s treatment downregulated the expression of genes involved in immune regulation and inflammation in dermal LECs without stress or stimulation.
source: Our results are in line with a previous report indicating that VEGFCc156s treatment downregulated the expression of genes involved in immune regulation and inflammation in dermal LECs without stress or stimulation (Dieterich et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Treatment of VEGFC induced a delayed systemic hemodynamic response to reduce blood pressure and attenuated related renal damage in a high-salt induced hypertension model.
source: Our observations are in line with a previous report indicating that the treatment of VEGFC, a ligand for both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3, also induced a delayed systemic hemodynamic response to reduce blood pressure and attenuated related renal damage in a high-salt induced hypertension model (Beaini et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Patients with hypertension have significantly lower serum VEGFC levels compared with healthy individuals.
source: Moreover, in line with the observations using the murine models, a recent clinical study also showed that patients with hypertension have significantly lower serum VEGFC levels compared with healthy individuals (Chachaj et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: Hypertension is a major risk factor for heart failure and other cardiovascular diseases.
source: Hypertension is a major risk factor for heart failure and other cardiovascular diseases (Dorans et al., 2018; Tackling and Borhade, 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Anti-hypertensive therapies significantly reduce cardiovascular events and mortality in patients in clinical studies.
source: and anti-hypertensive therapies significantly reduce cardiovascular events and mortality in patients in clinical studies (Ettehad et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to clinical studies.

claim: Renal lymphatics play a role in the pathogenesis of hypertension.
source: Consistent with previous reports regarding the role of renal lymphatics in the pathogenesis of hypertension (Balasubbramanian et al., 2020; Lopez Gelston et al., 2018), we also observed an endogenous expansion of renal lymphatics in response to angiotensin II-induced hypertension (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature and data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Enhancing renal lymphatic expansion by over-expressing VEGFD prevented the development of hypertension.
source: The previous reports also demonstrated that enhancing renal lymphatic expansion by over-expressing VEGFD prevented the development of hypertension.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to previous reports.

claim: Immune cells and inflammatory processes can play a role in the pathogenesis of hypertension.
source: Immune cells and inflammatory processes can play a role in the pathogenesis of hypertension (Caillon et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Skin lymphatics have been implicated as a potential disease-modifying factor in the pathogenesis of salt-sensitive hypertension.
source: Another possibility is that VEGFCc156s might affect the skin lymphatic vasculature to regulate blood pressure, as skin lymphatics have been implicated as a potential disease-modifying factor in the pathogenesis of salt-sensitive hypertension (Karlsen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The lymphatic vasculature has been proposed to play an important role in regulating myocardial fibrosis.
source: The lymphatic vasculature has been proposed to play an important role in regulating myocardial fibrosis (Brakenhielm et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lymphangiogenic factor treatment in a rat model of myocardial infarction improved cardiac function by reducing cardiac fibrosis.
source: and a previous report indicated that lymphangiogenic factor treatment in a rat model of myocardial infarction improved cardiac function by reducing cardiac fibrosis (Henri et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.
